full_judgment:
9. Mr. Ali then contended that the trial of the petitioner with three other persons stood vitiated because the petitioner as well as three other persons who were accused of different offences could not be tried together inasmuch as the offences said to have been committed by them were not committed in course of the same transaction and as such there was misjoinder of charges, joint trial having been held for separate and distinct offences. Both the courts over-ruled this contention. Section 233 of the Criminal Procedure Code lays down that for every distinct/ offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge and every such charge shall be tried separately except in the cases mentioned in Sections 234, 235, 236 and 239. It was argued that four advances alleged to have been given to the Contractor on four different dates were four distinct offences. Moreover, control of the sale of tender forms, acquisition of land and extension of the work were also separate and independent transactions and as such they were all distinct offences which having been tried together the trial was vitiated by misjoinder of charges. The learned Judge of the High Court having considered the provisions of Section 235 of the Cede of Criminal Procedure held that an accused might be charged with and tried at one trial for any number of offences alleged to have been committed in one series of acts so connected together as to form part of the same transaction. 

 11. We are of the view that the High Court has rightly found that the alleged several acts formed parts of the said transactions. In our opinion clause (d) of section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure seems to be the appropriate provisions of law applicable in the instant case as clause (d) of section 239 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides that persons accused of an offence and persons accused of abetment may be charged and tried together. The petitioner Zaker Hossain was charged as the principal accused and the other persons as abettors. Mr. Ali with a view to show that the trial of the petitioner held jointly with other accused was vitiated with illegality relied on the case of Babulal Chowkhani Vs. King Emperor, A.I.R. 1938 (P.C.) 130. That case arose out of theft of electricity under section 39 of the Electricity Act 1910. The Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation was, in the year 1934, concerned to find a discrepancy between units of energy generated and those accounted for by sales in excess of what would normally be experienced by the regular cases of wastage such as transmission or conversion losses. The Electric Supply Corporation of Calcutta having obtained sufficient prima facie materials lodged a complaint before the Chief Presidency Magistrate at Calcutta against 23 persons that their electricity was being stolen with particular reference to Babulal Chowkhani's cinema hall. On conclusion of the trial several persons including the appellant Babulal were convicted. On appeal to the High Court of Calcutta by Babulal Chowkhani his conviction for conspiracy was quashed. But the conviction under the main charge for theft of electricity was maintained. Then there was an appeal to the Privy Council. Before the Privy Council it was urged that offences which ought to have been separately charged were joined together. Hence the trial was bad in law. In that connection section 239(d) came up for consideration. It was held that where offences which ought to have been separately charged were joined together but the specific offences were satisfactorily proved by competent evidence, corroborated in all necessary respects and no miscarriage of justice was caused, the irregularity was cured under Sections 225 and 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Their Lordships did not find that such a trial was vitiated by illegality. According to their Lordships the question of the correctness of the joinder which depends on the sameness or the transaction is to be determined by looking at the accusation and not by looking at the result of the trial. It is on the basis of what appears on the face of the accusation that the court may proceed to charge and try. We do not see how this decision supports Mr. Ali. The trial of the petitioner with other accused was not vitiated by misjoinder of charges or of persons. Since the trial of the petitioner along with other accused was legally held, there is no force in the, Contention raised by Mr. Ali.
